reviews.early-cretaceous-epoch: The Early Cretaceous was shaped from below. Flood basalts and hotspots, from Paraná–Etendeka to Kerguelen and Ontong Java, helped tear Gondwana apart, opened the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and pumped out the carbon behind the Weissert warming and the Selli anoxic event. Climate swung between cold snaps with glacial dropstones and the start of the Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse. Through it all, life on land changed for good: flowering plants appeared and began to take over, pollinating insects coevolved with them, and grasses, ants and termites arrived. Fossil sites from Jehol and Las Hoyas to Crato and Burmese amber caught feathered dinosaurs, early birds and the first marsupial and placental relatives in the act.

cret-021.title: The Eastern Alps begin to stack up
cret-021.text: The Alps began to rise long before Africa and Europe actually collided. In the first, Eo-Alpine, mountain-building phase, from 140 to 84 million years ago, the Austroalpine nappes of the Eastern Alps were stacked like folded sheets of rock. Africa was moving toward Europe again, and ocean crust of the Piemont-Liguria Ocean was subducted beneath the Apulian plate. The first continental collision, of the Adriatic subplate with Europe, came in the Late Cretaceous. The main Alpine mountain building followed in the Paleocene–Eocene.

cret-025.title: The Sevier orogeny raises the western mountains
cret-025.text: Western North America's mountains rose over an extraordinarily long stretch. The Sevier orogeny ran from 140 to 50 million years ago. It has been tied to the continent's collision with a chain of island arcs about 125 million years ago. In Utah, the Willard thrust sheet moved around 120 million years ago. As the mountains rose in the west, the Western Interior Basin to the east widened.

cret-026.title: Cold spells bring ice to the Early Cretaceous
cret-026.text: The Mesozoic was long thought to be free of ice. The rocks disagree. As the cooling of the latest Jurassic continued into the Berriasian, snow fell often at high latitudes. Records suggest glacial periods in the Valanginian, Hauterivian and Aptian. Ice-rafted dropstones hint that Northern Hemisphere ice sheets may have reached as far south as Iberia in the Hauterivian and Aptian. Deposits laid down directly by glaciers, though, are known only from the Early Cretaceous of the Eromanga Basin in southern Australia. The early Barremian Hauptblatterton Thermal Event finally ended the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval.

cret-027.title: Titanosaurs, the last great sauropods, appear
cret-027.text: Titanosaur bones have been found on every continent, Antarctica included. This last great sauropod group lived from about 136 to 66 million years ago and was the dominant plant-eating group of its time. An early subadult from Paraíba, Brazil, is about 136 million years old. The group spread almost worldwide. Not all were giants: on the islands of Cretaceous Europe, some, such as Magyarosaurus, were likely island dwarfs.

cret-028.title: Paraná–Etendeka flood basalts pour out as Gondwana splits
cret-028.text: Its lavas covered about 1,000,000 km², from South America to Namibia and Angola. The Paraná–Etendeka large igneous province spans the Paraná Basin of South America and the split-off Etendeka traps of Africa. Its original volume is projected at over 2.3 million km³. These flood basalts erupted over the Tristan hotspot and were tied to Gondwana's rifting and the opening of the South Atlantic. Their activity caused a warming event, the middle Valanginian Weissert Thermal Excursion.

cret-030.title: Jehol: volcanic ash buries feathered dinosaurs
cret-030.text: The first known feathered dinosaurs that were not birds came out of lake beds in north-eastern China. The Jehol Biota is the ecosystem preserved there between 135 and 121 million years ago, in lake sediments and volcanic ash of the Yixian and Jiufotang formations. It holds many birds, the largest known Mesozoic mammals, the earliest known flowering plants, and insects, fish, pterosaurs and amphibians in huge numbers. It also has the earliest members of groups that later spread worldwide: neoceratopsians, therizinosaurs, tyrannosaurs and oviraptorids. Radiometric dating in 2021 placed the Yixian between 125.755 and 124.122 million years ago, a span of about 1.6 million years.

cret-031.title: The Weissert Event: a sudden heat spike
cret-031.text: In the middle of a mild, cool interval, the planet suddenly overheated. The Weissert Event was a hyperthermal, a rapid global warming. Carbon dioxide from the Paraná–Etendeka province is the leading suspected trigger, though its drawn-out eruption leads some to doubt it. Its carbon-isotope excursion began about 134.5 million years ago and its plateau lasted to about 132.4; estimates of its length run from 1.4 to 2.08 million years. The warming brought oceanic anoxia but, unusually, no widespread black shales, while nannoconid plankton bloomed as productivity soared. Its end brought sharp cooling, about 1–2 °C in southern France and up to 4 °C around the Boreal Ocean, perhaps even a brief ice age.

cret-032.title: The first flowering plants leave their pollen
cret-032.text:
The first flowers announced themselves with dust. The earliest widely accepted evidence of flowering plants is single-grooved pollen from the late Valanginian, about 134 million years ago, found in Israel and Italy. Flowering plants appeared in the Early Cretaceous and began to diversify rapidly, one of the major changes of the epoch.

Their oldest larger fossils come soon after. Montsechia grew in Barremian Spain, and Archaefructus, 124.6 million years old, comes from China's Yixian Formation. Pollen typical of eudicots, the largest modern branch, first appears in the late Barremian, and the earliest monocots, the grass and lily branch, are known from the Aptian. Flowering plants radiated first in the tropics. Then, helped by the gentle difference in temperature between equator and poles, they spread toward the poles.

cret-033.title: The Faraoni Event brings another warm pulse
cret-033.text: The Weissert Event was not the last of the Early Cretaceous warmings. In the middle Hauterivian came the next in the series, the Faraoni Thermal Excursion. A minor oceanic anoxic event, recorded mostly around the Atlantic, has also been proposed for the Hauterivian.

cret-034.title: Australia begins its slow parting from Antarctica
cret-034.text: Australia took tens of millions of years to leave Antarctica. Separation began about 132 million years ago, and by 96 million years ago the two had begun rifting, with seafloor spreading following. The Australian plate was born as it parted from Antarctica and Zealandia, a split finished in the Cenomanian. By 96 million years ago a shallow seaway had begun forming, leaving only a narrow link along the South Tasman Rise and Wilkes Land. A narrow land connection between South America, Antarctica and Australia lasted until about 50 million years ago. The general consensus places full separation by 60 million years ago.

cret-035.title: The first anglerfish appear
cret-035.text: Today's anglerfish dangle a lure in front of their mouths to catch prey. Their line is ancient. The earliest anglerfish appeared about 130 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous, while dinosaurs still walked the land.

cret-041.title: The South Atlantic begins to open
cret-041.text: Africa became an island continent, and stayed one through most of the Cenozoic. The South Atlantic started to open about 130 million years ago. The Falkland Plateau, broken from southern Africa at 132 million years ago, moved west. South America drifted west away from Africa, while Laurasia rotated clockwise and moved north. Paraná–Etendeka magmatism drove further seafloor spreading about 135–130 million years ago, south of the Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise. The split also opened the West and Central African Rift System, including the Benue Trough. By the Aptian–Albian, Africa was cut off from the rest of Gondwana and Laurasia.

cret-038.title: India breaks loose from Australia and Antarctica
cret-038.text: India's long voyage north began with a break from its southern neighbors. Between 130 and 125 million years ago, the Indian plate broke off from Australia and Antarctica, opening the 'South Indian Ocean'. The Indian Ocean began opening about 130 million years ago, its spreading ridge near the Kerguelen hotspot. Rifts along East Africa, Antarctica and Madagascar formed the southwestern Indian Ocean, and later India and Madagascar began to part. Madagascar stopped moving independently around 120 million years ago.

cret-039.title: North China's craton loses its deep root
cret-039.text: Cratons are usually the most stable parts of a continent, but North China's lost its foundation. Around 130–120 million years ago, tectonics there switched to extension, its mountain belts and plateau collapsed, and the deep mantle root was replaced. Retreating Paleo-Pacific subduction may have thinned the craton's lithosphere. A large igneous province on the Liaodong Peninsula was active about 131–117 million years ago.

cret-040.title: Colombia's Paja shales preserve sea reptiles
cret-040.text: The world's most complete record of Early Cretaceous marine reptiles lies in Colombia. Its shales and mudstones settled in a warm, shallow, anoxic sea that covered much of the present-day country. The IUGS, the international geology body, lists the Paja Formation as a geological heritage site for that record.

cret-037.title: High Arctic magma helps open the Arctic Ocean
cret-037.text: Even after much has eroded, its lavas still cover more than 1,000,000 km². The High Arctic Large Igneous Province, or HALIP, is one of Earth's largest magmatic complexes, active from 130 million years ago to about 60 million. Its first phase ran to 80 million years ago with dikes, sills and basalt flows. It broke up part of the Arctica continent, opened the Arctic Ocean and left radiating dike swarms. Crustal stretching began in the Canadian Arctic Rift System 130 million years ago, with widespread sills and dikes intruded 129–127 million years ago. The Iceland hotspot may have started as a plume under the Alpha Ridge about 130–120 million years ago.

cret-042.title: Tookoonooka: a crater buried deep in Australia
cret-042.text: Deep beneath Australia's Eromanga Basin lies a crater 55–66 km across. Shocked quartz in drill core proved that an impact made it, about 128 ± 5 million years ago. The nearby Talundilly structure may be its twin.

cret-043.title: A Belgian coal mine full of Iguanodon
cret-043.text: At least 38 Iguanodon skeletons turned up deep in a coal mine at Bernissart, Belgium, in the Sainte-Barbe Clays Formation. Iguanodon bernissartensis, the one well-supported species, lived in Europe about 126–122 million years ago and grew to about 9 m long. The bones were once read as a herd that died together. They now seem to record at least three separate die-offs, probably from flash floods.

cret-045.title: Earliest marsupial and placental relatives appear in China
cret-045.text: Two small mammals from the same Chinese shale stand at the base of two great branches. Sinodelphys, from 125-million-year-old rocks in Liaoning, is the earliest known metatherian, the marsupial line, and it had climbing feet. Eomaia, a eutherian of the same age, shared features with marsupials that the placental line later lost. Both already stood with upright, non-sprawling limbs. Other therian mammals are unknown before the Early Cretaceous, and even the Jurassic Juramaia may itself be Early Cretaceous. The finds suggest early mammals began to diversify from Asia.

cret-047.title: Las Hoyas preserves a Spanish wetland in stone
cret-047.text: About 125 million years ago, a freshwater wetland in Spain turned into fine limestone. At Las Hoyas, it preserves dinosaurs and many enantiornithine birds in exquisite detail. It also yields Montsechia, one of the oldest flowering-plant fossils larger than pollen.

cret-046.title: Flowers and pollinators remake life on land
cret-046.text:
For nearly all of Earth's history, the sea held more species than the land. In the mid-Cretaceous, that reversed. The change came with the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution, from around 125 to 80 million years ago. In it, flowering plants diversified intensely alongside the pollinating insects that coevolved with them.

Animal-pollinated flowers set off a burst of coevolution. Beetles were pollinating by the earliest Late Cretaceous, and moths and butterflies have coevolved with flowers ever since. By 110–90 million years ago, flowering plants dominated forest trees. By the period's end they had displaced conifers, cycads and bennettitaleans, though full ecological dominance came only in the early Cenozoic. Their spread may have sped up weathering and nutrient flow into the oceans, a possible driver of the {{ref:tria-014}}.

cret-044.title: Stressed forests pour out resin, and amber piles up
cret-044.text: Trees bleed resin when they are hurt, and Cretaceous trees were hurt often. From 125 to 75 million years ago, heat-driven storms, hurricanes, wildfires and insect damage made them produce huge amounts of it. By the Early Cretaceous, amber, fossilized resin, formed in concentrations matching or exceeding those of the Carnian.

cret-049.title: Koolasuchus, the last temnospondyl amphibian
cret-049.text: The temnospondyls had outlived the end-Permian and end-Triassic crises, and their last stand came in Australia. Koolasuchus, a chigutisaurid from the Aptian, is the latest known temnospondyl. Stereospondyls, including brachyopoids, had survived from the Triassic into the Cretaceous. All were gone by the Late Cretaceous, leaving lissamphibians, the frogs, salamanders and their kin, as the only amphibians.

cret-050.title: Thalattosuchian sea crocodiles fade away
cret-050.text: In the Jurassic, sea-going crocodile relatives called thalattosuchians were abundant. By the Early Cretaceous they had become scarce and mostly tropical. Their last records come from the Aptian, and after that this long marine experiment of the crocodile line was over.

cret-051.title: The plated stegosaurs make their last stand
cret-051.text: As seaways spread in the Early Cretaceous, the high-browsers lost ground. Sauropods, stegosaurs and other groups that fed high above the ground declined. The youngest definitive stegosaurs, including Mongolostegus from Mongolia and Yanbeilong from China, date to the Aptian–Albian. Stegosaurs appear to have died out in the late Early or early Late Cretaceous. Reported later finds have mostly proved misidentified.

cret-052.title: Earth's magnetic field stops flipping for 37 million years
cret-052.text: For about 37 million years, compasses would have pointed the same way. From the Aptian through the Santonian, Earth's magnetic field kept normal polarity with no reversals. On the calibrated time scale, this superchron, chron C34n, began at 120.964 million years ago and ended at 83.650. Reversals had grown steadily rarer in the run-up to it. It is one of two well-established superchrons, alongside the Permian Kiaman. All Ontong Java Plateau lavas are normally magnetized, so they presumably erupted after it began.

cret-053.title: The Selli Event chokes the oceans of oxygen
cret-053.text: Perhaps 9,000 Gt of carbon, released by magma intruding beneath the Barents Sea, may have set it off. At the start of the Aptian, the Selli Event, or OAE1a, stripped oxygen from oceans worldwide. Tied to large-igneous-province volcanism, it killed marine life through warming, acidification and oxygen loss. Its carbon-isotope shift began within 22,000–47,000 years. The event lasted about 1.1–1.3 million years, and recovery took over a million more. With OAE2, it was one of the two Cretaceous anoxic events that most changed ocean chemistry, leaving black shales worldwide.

cret-055.title: Egg-laying monotremes appear in Australia
cret-055.text: The platypus has very old roots in Australia. Teinolophos, which lived there about 120 million years ago, is one of the earliest known monotremes, the egg-laying mammals. Steropodon, from Australia about 105 million years ago, has also been called the oldest monotreme.

cret-057.title: The last mammal-like tritylodontids vanish
cret-057.text: Some cynodonts came so close to being mammals that they are called extremely mammal-like. Tritylodontids, plant-eaters, were the last surviving cynodonts outside the mammaliaforms. In Asia they persisted into the Barremian–Aptian, at least until around 120 million years ago, as Fossiomanus from China shows. They died out in the Early Cretaceous.

cret-059.title: A small impact scars Ukraine
cret-059.text: A crater just 2.7 km wide lies at Rotmistrivka in Ukraine. It is dated to 120 ± 10 million years ago. Under Early Cretaceous sediments, it holds a lens of granite breccia, broken rock cemented together, and impact glass.

cret-056.title: The Kerguelen hotspot piles up a giant plateau
cret-056.text: About 25 million km³ of lava built a plateau in the southern Indian Ocean. The Kerguelen hotspot's output peaked 120–95 million years ago, building the Southern and Central Kerguelen Plateau and Broken Ridge, which together cover 2,300,000 km². Its earliest products include Australia's Bunbury Basalt, 137–130.5 million years old. India's Rajmahal and Sylhet Traps, 118–115 million years old, came next, linked to the opening of the eastern Indian Ocean. Growth of the Southern Kerguelen Plateau 118–119 million years ago contributed to oceanic anoxic event 1. The Kerguelen microcontinent may even have carried dense conifer forest in the mid-Cretaceous.

cret-060.title: The Aptian–Albian Cold Snap chills the planet
cret-060.text: Global mean surface temperature fell to about 20.7 °C. After the Barremian–Aptian Warm Interval, the Aptian–Albian Cold Snap began about 118 million years ago. Glacial dropstones in western Tethys sediments hint at an ice age. The cold ended around 111 million years ago with the Paquier/Urbino Thermal Maximum.

cret-061.title: A minor extinction strikes the Aptian seas
cret-061.text: Around 116 or 117 million years ago, a minor extinction struck, seen mostly in marine rocks. It may be linked to the Rajmahal Traps eruptions in India, fed by the Kerguelen hotspot. Minor as it was, for the history of plants it is an important episode, deserving more weight than other small events.

cret-062.title: Ontong Java: the greatest eruption in 200 million years
cret-062.text:
Up to 22 km³ of magma a year, for 3 million years. The 'Ontong Java event' was the largest volcanic event of the past 200 million years. The Ontong Java, Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus in the south-west Pacific probably formed as one contiguous large igneous province, by far Earth's largest. When the eruptions ended, it covered 1% of Earth's surface with 80 million km³ of basalt, several times the Deccan Traps.

The Ontong Java Plateau formed around 116 million years ago, with a much smaller event around 90 million years ago. Renewed rifting about 116 million years ago split Manihiki from Hikurangi. The eruptions were long thought to coincide with OAE1a, the Selli Event. But basalt ages of 117–108 million years and the lavas' normal magnetization make that unlikely.

cret-064.title: Subduction zones begin to ring the Pacific
cret-064.text: The Pacific Ring of Fire, today's loop of volcanoes and earthquakes, began to take shape in the Early Cretaceous. About 120–115 million years ago, the Farallon plate was subducting beneath the Americas and north-east Asia, and the Izanagi plate beneath east Asia. By about 115 million years ago, today's subduction zones had begun to form the ring around South America, North America and Asia.

cret-065.title: Vista Alegre crater scars Brazil's basalts
cret-065.text: An impact punched into the basalt plains of southern Brazil, near the Vargeão Dome. Geologists have recently dated this Vista Alegre crater to about 115 million years ago.

cret-063.title: Deinonychus: the sickle claw that remade dinosaur science
cret-063.text: One dinosaur changed how scientists imagine all the others. Deinonychus, a dromaeosaurid up to 3.4 m long with a large sickle-shaped claw on each foot, lived in North America about 115–98 million years ago. Its 1969 description revealed an active, agile predator, launching the 'dinosaur renaissance' and a debate over warm-blooded dinosaurs. Its bird-like forelimbs led Ostrom to revive the idea that birds descend from dinosaurs, now almost universally accepted.

cret-067.title: The first grasses take root
cret-067.text: Grasses, the plants of lawns and prairies, first appear in the fossil record in the Albian. Those are the oldest known grass fossils. By the end of the Cretaceous, grasses had already diversified into modern groups.

cret-068.title: Brazil's Crato lake preserves soft parts in stone
cret-068.text: Fish from Brazil's Crato Formation still hold their last meals. The formation was laid down about 113 million years ago in a semi-arid lake wetland, where limestone nodules formed around carcasses and preserved soft parts and stomach contents. With the Romualdo Formation, it makes up the Santana beds of north-east Brazil, which preserve pterosaurs, fish, invertebrates and plants exceptionally well. Lying near the ancient equator, they are key sites for Early Cretaceous insects.

cret-070.title: Borealopelta, an armored dinosaur 'mummy' from Alberta
cret-070.text: Pigments in its skin suggest Borealopelta was reddish-brown and countershaded, darker above and lighter below. That camouflage implies even this 5.5 m armored nodosaurid faced predators. After death, it washed out to sea and was buried in marine sands and shales of Alberta's Clearwater Formation about 110–112 million years ago. It is among the best-preserved dinosaurs of its size, keeping armor, keratin sheaths, skin and stomach contents.

cret-069.title: More anoxic events strike the Albian seas
cret-069.text: The Albian oceans lost their oxygen again and again. Further oceanic anoxic events, OAE1b, 1c and 1d, struck around 112–100 million years ago. Their black shales lie mostly in the Atlantic region, and some researchers blame local conditions rather than global change. They fall within one of the longest anoxic intervals in geologic history, about 125–80 million years ago, perhaps paced by orbital cycles.

cret-071.title: Snakes emerge from their lizard ancestors
cret-071.text: The oldest true snakes swam in the sea. They are marine simoliophiids such as the Cenomanian Haasiophis from the West Bank, dated 112–94 million years ago, though timelines of life put snake origins near 90. Najash, about 95 million years old, kept a lizard-like skull with some of the mobile joints of modern snakes. Tetrapodophis, 113 million years old and hailed as a snake in 2015, was later placed among lizards. Snakes evolved from lizards, perhaps burrowers or mosasaur relatives, and in the Late Cretaceous they recolonized land and kept diversifying.

cret-073.title: The Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse switches on
cret-073.text: Late Albian tropical seas averaged about 30 °C. Temperatures rose sharply after the cold snap ended around 111 million years ago, opening the Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse, which lasted until the early Campanian. A string of Albian hyperthermals followed: Leenhardt at about 110 million years ago, l'Arboudeyesse, Amadeus at about 106, Event 6 at about 102.5 and Breistroffer at about 101. Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera show gradual warming from the Albian to peak warmth in the Turonian. On land, arid belts repeatedly pushed north. In the Cloverly Formation, cool conditions lingered until a late-Albian warming pulse brought on the hothouse.

cret-072.title: Giganotosaurus prowls Patagonia
cret-072.text: Giganotosaurus rivaled Tyrannosaurus among the largest predators ever. This huge carcharodontosaurid lived in Argentina about 111–106 million years ago. A 2026 study re-dated its rock formations from the Cenomanian to the early Albian. Its South American lineage may have been split from African relatives as Gondwana broke up in the Aptian–Albian.

cret-075.title: South America and Africa finally let go
cret-075.text: Identical dinosaur footprints in Brazil and Cameroon, about 120 million years old, suggest the two continents were still linked by land in the early Aptian. North of the equator, rifting began after 120.4 million years ago and lasted until about 100–96 million years ago; the Benue Trough rifted about 118 million years ago. By 110 million years ago, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge reached the Proto-Caribbean and South Atlantic, separating South America from Africa and completing the Atlantic's length. The breakup may have split South America's carcharodontosaurids from their African relatives. Around 100 million years ago, South Atlantic spreading sped up sharply. The ridge grew from 1,200 to 7,000 km, and Africa began moving north-east.

cret-076.title: Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan, the titanosaur giants
cret-076.text: Argentinosaurus was about 30–35 m long and weighed 65–80 tonnes, among the largest land animals ever. It comes from Argentina's Huincul Formation, which a 2026 study placed in the Albian, about 106 million years ago; earlier work suggested a younger Cenomanian–Turonian age. Its close relative Patagotitan, from Patagonia's Cerro Barcino Formation, comes from rocks about 101.62 million years old. Patagotitan was first billed as the largest land animal, at 37 m and 69 tonnes. Later estimates cut it to about 31 m and 50–60 tonnes. Both belong to the titanosaurs, the dominant sauropods of the Cretaceous.

cret-077.title: Dinosaurs endure the polar night at Dinosaur Cove
cret-077.text: Inside the Antarctic Circle, small dinosaurs lived through the polar winter. Dinosaur Cove's fossil beds, about 106 million years old, formed on a rift-valley floodplain as Australia began to separate from Antarctica. Its 'polar dinosaurs' include small plant-eaters such as Leaellynasaura and Atlascopcosaurus, and one fossil hints at adaptations to low light. The poles were seasonally cold but much milder than today's, and some dinosaurs lived in the polar forests year-round.

cret-078.title: The granite of Half Dome and El Capitan forms
cret-078.text: Half Dome and El Capitan are cooled magma from the Cretaceous. As the Farallon plate subducted beneath North America, rising magma built the plutons of the Sierra Nevada Batholith, and most of its granite formed 105–85 million years ago. Subduction flattened about 80–76 million years ago, shutting down arc magmatism, and pluton formation ended around 70 million years ago. Uplift and erosion later exposed the batholith as the granite peaks of the High Sierra, Mount Whitney among them.

cret-079.title: Burmese amber traps a lost island world
cret-079.text: Chimerarachne, a 100-million-year-old arachnid, had silk spinnerets and a tail. It is one of over 1,000 species, mostly insects, found in Burmese amber from Myanmar's Hukawng Valley, 101–99 million years old. The amber formed on the Burma terrane, then an island in the Tethys Ocean near the equator, and preserves its small life in exquisite detail. Its trade is ethically controversial.
